title: The little grey man
sentences: Poor old fellow!
as if I can still see him…
When in December, on a cold, frosty night, he rode ahead of us in a simple grey cloak and tight gaiters; on one side of his face a still fresh wound was only roughly bandaged.
Most of the young army hardly had any clothes, and the unpleasant winter weather showed us little pity,
we were hungry too, as much as we could bear; but who would have dared to feel cold, who would have dared to complain then,
when the little grey man, in simple, thin clothing, without food or sleep, rode at the head in winter, in snow, on stormy nights?
We had no rest.
Hardly had we stopped in one place when we already heard his urging voice.
With a foreign accent, but with genuine fervour, he said each time: "Forward, forward!"
And who would have fallen behind, who would have grown weary,
when the little grey man, with his open wounds, without food or sleep, rode at the head in winter, in snow, on stormy nights?
Poor old fellow!
as if I can still see him…
When in January they took his cannons, on a long, rocky road one of his wagons overturned, and all the cannons left behind were lost because of it.
Enemy in front, enemy behind, and he had only four cannons and two thousand soldiers left.
All day, all night the little grey man fought the enemy, now in front, now behind, wherever he was attacked.
With his four cannons he defended himself, now here, now there under siege, and meanwhile the army marched forward in blood, in fire, in enemy country.
We reached a town; there they surrounded us.
It was midnight.
At midnight a messenger came from the enemy camp to call upon the little grey man to surrender.
He came out to us in the market square, lined up his army, looked them over and asked:
"Do you wish to continue fighting with me, or will you lay down your arms?
Will you come where I lead you?"
And who would not have gone with him when they saw him at the head?
A unanimous shout proclaimed that there was no one who would lay down his arms!…
"Go back" — the little grey man then said to the messenger —,
and tell your commander that I have already been surrounded twelve times; now I am surrounded for the thirteenth.
All twelve times I fought my way out…
Then they set the enemy town ablaze around us; the little grey man had his powder wagons covered with wet blankets,
and with that he galloped forward, behind him the little army with bayonets fixed, "Forward, forward!"
rang his cry, and who would not have followed him when they saw him galloping at the head in blood, in fire, in enemy country?
We came to a bridge.
Here the little grey man halted his army.
We go no further!
— he said, and turned to face the sea of enemies.
"If this bridge is lost, Transylvania is lost!"
— he said, arranging his troops on the bridge, and when in the crossfire one of his fingers was shot off,
with cool composure he had the maimed limb cut off, still sitting on his horse and directing his cannons.
The doctor fainted after the operation, but the little grey man smiled and said: I never got much use out of that finger anyway.
For a day and a half the little army fought against tremendous force above the bloody bridge,
half of the good lads fell, but not one fled, and whoever had his hand or leg shot off
thought of the little grey man, who had himself amputated with cool composure while sitting on his horse, and then did not moan.
A month later the little grey man fought below Sibiu.
He defeated the enemy, took the town, and when he had taken it, his first act was — to grant an amnesty.
"I did not come to make war on unarmed men, women and children."
And who would not have extended his hand to his mortal enemy for peace,
when the little grey man was the first to extend his own, on which only four fingers remained from the nearest battle?
But the little grey man was not right after all.
In a constitutional country a commander must not do such a thing.
To show mercy without the government's knowledge!
That is sheer tyranny.
Wherefore the little grey man, before they praised him for his victories, was sharply rebuked for the amnesty he had granted.
The little grey man, when he received the reprimand, replied to it
that all was well, but they should send money as soon as possible, because the soldiers were in rags.
Up there, therefore, to comply with this request, they made a golden order of merit for the little grey man, and before the colours of the national assembly appointed him lieutenant general.
At the same time they also appointed several other patriots lieutenant general, and the remaining judges of the table — some as colonel, some as major.
From this one may imagine what a great honour it must have been then to receive a military decoration.
An old, grey hussar colonel — the minister of war's aide — was entrusted with this appointment and the delivery of the decoration.
The little grey man was then in Kolozsvár.
The Saxons had just handed him a hundred thousand silver forints, which he distributed among his soldiers down to the last penny,
and the Transylvanian ladies a splendid embroidered horse blanket, which he never dared to sit on, but kept carefully stored away.
All this happened on the same day.
It was plain that this day was a day for winning gifts.
So it was that on that day the assembly's messenger also appeared with the dispatch case of credentials.
The old hussar colonel enters to see him.
He was a grey, tall man of about seventy.
When he saw the general, he stepped up to him, bowed to his maimed hand, and though an old, aged soldier, he kissed that hand browned in battle.
The little grey man, weeping, pressed the old grey soldier to his breast, and when the tender embrace ended,
the old hussar colonel addressed to him a very fine speech — in genuine German.
The good old hussar was a Hungarian born in Debrecen, who had spent a whole week preparing to deliver those German words,
and in the end he delivered them in such a way that anyone who did not know Hungarian could safely believe he was speaking Hungarian now.
The speech had some very moving passages.
At those passages the old hussar's eyes again involuntarily filled with tears.
His tears also stirred kindred feelings in the general; the little grey man wept, sensitively,
bitterly; he went up to the old hussar when he had finished his speech, warmly shook his hand trembling with emotion and said:
"Indeed, all that was very fine.
I shall forever regret that I do not know Hungarian, and could not understand a word of it; I beg you, translate for me into German what you spoke."
Until now not one of those present had failed to weep,
but at that moment it was impossible for the mood of the scene not to turn to the heartiest laughter.
The little grey man had listened through the entire sweat-of-the-brow German recitation believing
that the powerful, resonant Hungarian word was speaking to him.
The old hussar therefore wrote down on paper the words he had spoken, and presented them thus to the general.
He read them through, and nodded contentedly with his little grey head, but when he reached the passage
where the old hussar begins to praise the legions of the philhungarok, he put down the writing:
"This must be struck out" — he said — "only the Hungarian and the Székely are soldiers!"
Perhaps he was not right, but he loved the Hungarians so very much.
He loved them more than his own nation.
And then he gladly allowed the modest medal of merit to be pinned on him.
Yet in all his emotion, in his benevolent joy, he did not forget at the end of the ceremony to put to the assembly's messenger the question
which had already hovered on his lips when the man entered.
"Did you bring money for the soldiers?…"
"Not a thing this time."
"I would have wished you had, for I do not allow my boys either to plunder or to go without."
He would have spent both Indies on them!
that is how he loved them!
Poor old fellow!
As if I can still see him…
